title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement:
Given an unsorted integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **kth largest** value in it, the value that would sit at position `k` (1-based) if the array were sorted from largest to smallest.

Duplicates count separately: in `[7, 7, 1]` the 2nd largest is `7`.

target.note: a size-k min-heap is O(n log k); sorting is O(n log n); quickselect averages O(n)

hints: You only care about the k largest values. If you kept just those, which of them would be the answer?
Keep a min-heap holding the k largest values seen so far. Its top is the smallest of them, which is exactly the kth largest. When a bigger value arrives, it pushes the top out.
PriorityQueue<Integer> (a min-heap by default). For each x, offer it, and if the size goes over k, poll. At the end, peek. The heap never holds more than k + 1 values.
followups: Can you get O(n) average time? Explain quickselect with Lomuto or Hoare partitioning, and what its worst case is.
What if the numbers arrive as a stream and you have to report the kth largest after every new one?
When is the heap better than quickselect? Think about memory, streaming, and a k that is small compared with n.
explain: Keep a min-heap of size k. Every value goes in, and whenever the heap grows past k the smallest is evicted, so afterwards it holds exactly the k largest values and its top is the kth largest. O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Sorting and indexing n - k is a fine O(n log n) first answer. The optimal answer is quickselect: partition around a random pivot and recurse only into the side that contains index n - k. That's O(n) on average, O(n^2) worst case (a random pivot makes the worst case unlikely), and O(1) extra space if done in place. In Java, PriorityQueue is a min-heap. For a max-heap pass Collections.reverseOrder(), and never write a comparator as (a, b) -> b - a, which overflows near the int limits.
